## Chapter 74: Interactions, Multi-Level Factorials, and Building Experiments

### The Importance of Understanding Interactions

Chapter 73 briefly touched on the concept of interactions. Remember, one reason design of experiments is such a powerful tool for Six Sigma teams is that it doesn't just let practitioners analyze how certain factors and levels impact outcomes. Design of experiments also lets you understand how the combination of certain factors and levels impacts outcomes. Since designed experiments run every factor and level against every other factor and level, they can reveal interactions that other types of analysis, which only consider one factor at a time, might miss. Understanding interactions helps Six Sigma teams arrive at the strongest possible solution, while mitigating possible issues like waste or error.

In the sample healthcare experiment run in the previous chapter, there wasn't much interaction between the individual factors, but the interaction plots showed a slight interaction between the training and shift factors. If a team member had received compliance training in the last 6 months, they were more likely to comply with sanitization procedures. If the team member, who'd received the training in the last 6 months, was also within the first four hours of a shift, the increase in compliance probability associated with the training was slightly larger than the same increase in someone past four hours into a shift.

Interactions are shown on interaction plots by lines that aren't parallel. The less parallel the lines are, the greater the interaction. As you can see, most of these lines are close to parallel, meaning any interaction that exists here is fairly weak. Consider the bottom-left chart. The blue line shows measurements taken when the department was below 80 percent patient capacity. The red line shows measurements taken when the department was above 80 percent patient capacity. Regardless of capacity status, the measurements' behavior is basically the same, depending on whether the team member received compliance training in the last six months or not. That means there isn't much interaction — one factor's setting doesn't seem to impact how the other factor's settings change the outcome.

<img alt="Minitab "Fit Linear Model for Compliance — Effects Report" (higher-resolution crop): Interaction Plots for Compliance, showing the three panels StaffEd*TimeShift, StaffEd*NoPts, TimeShift*NoPts with nearly parallel lines, indicating little interaction" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### Understanding the Main Effect

To better understand how interactions are measured, you first need to understand the main effect. Consider a real-world example, again with a 2-level factorial. In this example, a Six Sigma team within a movie theater chain is trying to positively impact concession-stand performance. Specifically, the team has been tasked with increasing concession-stand profits.

One area the team is focusing on is the popcorn-making process, and they've identified waste as a root cause of the problem in that part of the concession stand. The team believes the current popcorn-making process is generating waste, because many of the kernels introduced into the popcorn machine never pop. Those kernels are regularly swept out of the machine and thrown away, and the team believes the amount of kernels thrown away every day equals at least 10 large popcorn orders.

While that might seem like a small amount of waste, the team calculates that the concession stand earns a $2.65 profit on each large popcorn order, meaning the stand is losing roughly $9,600 a year on lost popcorn kernels. If the team can use a designed experiment to identify a fast, cheap way to reduce kernel waste, it might be worth the effort.

After learning more about the kernel process, the team decides the machine's temperature at the moment popcorn is introduced is a factor. They also decide the number of kernels placed in the machine and the popcorn brand are factors too.

The team designs the following experiment:

*(Table: 8 combinations — Row 1-8 — crossing Brand (A, B), Temperature (400°F, 600°F), and Kernels (1 scoop, 2 scoops), a full 2³ factorial.)*

Following good experiment protocol, the team decides on sample size. Remember, sample size for a designed experiment is what tells you how many replications of the overall experiment to run. In this case, the Six Sigma team decides to run 4 replications. Given the design above, that means the team will log 32 runs. Also following good experiment protocol, the team randomizes the runs, so as not to log the information in the same order every time throughout the experiment.

The Six Sigma practitioner on the team also knew that simply logging the amount of kernels left over after each batch wouldn't let them draw statistical conclusions about the three factors the team was considering. That's because one of the factors the team was considering was the volume of kernels going into the process. Naturally, if more kernels go into the process, there's likely to be more waste kernels — the team shouldn't need an experiment to test whether that's true. The team really wants to find out whether a larger proportion of unpopped kernels remains when popping one or two scoops of certain popcorn brands at certain temperatures. The Six Sigma practitioner makes sure the team logs both the total number of kernels and the percentage, or proportion, of those kernels relative to the number of kernels that went into the process.

The information the team logged is shown in the table below. Note the data was sorted by brand, then temperature, then number of scoops, for analysis purposes. That wouldn't be the order the team ran the experiment in, since it would have been randomized.

*(Data table: 32 runs — Row Number, Brand (A/B), Temperature (400°F/600°F), Kernels (1/2 scoops), Est. No Kernels (2300 or 4600), Kernels Left, Percent Left — with 4 replications for each of the 8 combinations, percentages ranging from 2.13% to 8.67%.)*

The effect, in a designed experiment, is the measurement of the change in outcome based on the change in factor levels. The main effect describes the measurement of the change in outcome based on changes in a single factor. Each individual factor's main effect can be roughly calculated by comparing the average outcome at both the low and high ends of the factor.

For example, the average percent remaining for Brand A is 4.45. The average remaining for Brand B is 4.36. The difference is 0.09. Right away, it looks like there isn't much of an effect on kernel-popping performance between the two popcorn brands. Remember, though, that a statistical difference doesn't necessarily require a large numerical difference. Whether the difference is worth considering depends on other factors, like the range of difference the team expects to log and other factors' main effect in the experiment.

The same calculation can be made for each of the factors in the experiment. The average percent of kernels remaining for runs at 400 degrees F is roughly 5.43; the average remaining for runs at 600 degrees F is 3.38. The main effect for this factor is bigger than for brand; the difference between the averages for 400 degrees and 600 degrees is 2.05.

The average percent of kernels remaining when the team started with one scoop was roughly 3.27. The percent remaining when starting with two scoops was roughly 5.54; the difference is 2.27.

> Here, it's worth noting that the team made an assumption. The team, in this example, didn't count the number of kernels in each scoop before running the popcorn process. Instead, they assumed one scoop of popcorn kernels contained 2,300 kernels. The fact that not every scoop will have exactly 2,300 kernels could impact the experiment's outcome. Why would a Six Sigma team make such an assumption, if it could impact the experiment?
>
> In Chapter 73, the possible expense of designed experiments was mentioned. The time and resources needed to run an experiment play a role in whether a team or Six Sigma practitioner chooses to use that tool for analysis. But time and resources can also play a role in how a team designs an experiment and what assumptions and steps it takes when setting factors. In this example, running 64 separate batches of popcorn would be fairly time-consuming, but likely not time-consuming enough to be prohibitive. It also wouldn't be very expensive in terms of resource use, especially if the team runs the runs in a way that lets the popcorn generated by the runs be used in the concession stand's service.
>
> However, if the team counted every individual popcorn kernel going into the process, two things could happen. First, the team could spend a disproportionate amount of time counting what would ultimately be more than 220,000 popcorn kernels. Remember, the savings that might result from this experiment are estimated at only roughly $9,600 a year. There's probably not enough return on investment for the team to spend that much time counting kernels. Second, the team could actually impact the kernels' quality through the excessive handling that could occur during counting. That could lower how effectively the kernels popped, impacting the experiment's authenticity. Teams and Six Sigma practitioners should always try to avoid impacting an experiment's outcomes in ways not directly related to setting various factors' levels.
>
> Sometimes, you might have to make assumptions when running experiments. When you do, you should always try to handle measurements and assumptions according to all the information provided throughout this book. For example, a Six Sigma practitioner would never simply decide that one scoop equals 2,300 kernels. Some ways you could arrive at that assumption include:
> - Counting how many kernels are in several scoops and arriving at an average (remember that sample size and confidence levels would play a role in how confident you could be in that average)
> - Weighing 50 separate kernels to get an average weight for one popcorn kernel, then weighing several scoops to see how many kernels, based on weight, might be included (again, sample size and confidence levels would play a role in how you'd treat these assumptions).
>

### Understanding Interaction Plots

When plotted on a line chart, the main effects from the experiment above look like the image below. These images are generated in Excel, but Minitab and other statistical analysis software generate these charts as part of the overall analysis when running designed experiments.

<img alt="Line chart "Main Effects Chart" generated in Excel, showing Brand (nearly flat), Temperature (sharp drop from Low to High), and Scoops (sharp rise from Low to High)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:474px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


This image makes it easy to see: there isn't much of a main effect for popcorn brand, but there are important changes based on temperature and scoop. Since the team wants to reduce the percentage of unpopped kernels, it looks like they'll want to set the temperature at a higher level, but use only one scoop of popcorn at a time.

But the main-effects chart doesn't always account for any interaction between factors, which is why it's important to consider interaction plots. You can use Minitab to generate interaction plots, or build your own in Excel 365. The most direct path in Excel 365 skips the old workflow's manual series editing — just arrange the data into a small "pivoted" table and let Excel detect the series automatically:

1. Calculate the average outcome for each two-factor combination with `=AVERAGEIFS(` — for example, for Kernels=1 and Temperature=400: `=AVERAGEIFS(PercentLeft, Kernels, 1, Temperature, 400)`.
2. Arrange the results into a table pivoted by factor pair, with one factor's levels in rows and the other factor's levels in separate columns — like this:

1. Select the entire table (headers included) and choose **Insert → Charts → Insert Line or Area Chart → Line with Markers**. Since the first column becomes the category axis and each following column automatically becomes a series, there's no need to open "Select Data" or manually edit series or axis labels.
2. Repeat for the other two factor pairs (Kernels × Brand, Brand × Temperature). All three results are shown below.

<img alt="Three interaction charts generated in Excel side by side: "Scoop * Temperature", "Temperature * Brand", and "Scoops * Brand", each comparing two line series" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


These are the same style of interaction plots Minitab displays, if you run a DOE analysis in that program, and they show some interaction that wasn't apparent just from looking at the raw data or even the main-effects charts.

Analysis of the first interaction plot shows what the Six Sigma team might have already noticed from the main effects. The lowest percentage of remaining kernels seems to come when you combine 1 scoop of kernels and the higher temperature setting. This chart shows no interaction — the lines are nearly parallel. Regardless of the number of scoops you start with, the higher temperature produces the least waste. Regardless of the temperature setting, starting with the lower scoop amount produces the least waste.

The second chart, to the right of the first, shows the interaction between brand and temperature. Remember, the main-effects analysis seemed to indicate that popcorn-brand choice didn't matter. When brand is analyzed against another factor, though, that doesn't seem to hold. In this chart, you can see brand makes a difference in how the change in temperature setting plays out.

At 600 degrees F, brand A performs better than brand B. At 400 degrees F, brand B performs better. Even so, both brands generate less waste at the higher temperature setting, compared to their own performance at the lower temperature setting.

The third chart also shows some interaction between brand and number of scoops. Brand B performs better at the lower scoop setting than brand A, and the reverse holds at the higher setting. Again, both brands generate less waste at the lower scoop setting, compared to their own performance at the higher setting.

Based on all the information above, the Six Sigma team will likely choose to start the popcorn process with 1 scoop and use the 600 degrees F temperature setting. Choosing a popcorn brand, though, is a bit harder. Going with brand A saves roughly 0.5 percent in waste over brand B, when considering the interaction with temperature. However, brand B saves nearly 1 percent in waste over brand A, when considering the interaction with number of scoops.

Given all the information and analysis from this experiment, a Six Sigma team might say brand isn't a big enough factor (so the concession stand could choose the brand based on other factors, like cost) or recommend that brand B be purchased whenever it's equal to or cheaper than brand A, since brand B is associated with the higher percentage of waste savings. If brand B were more expensive than brand A, the small waste savings associated with brand B would likely be canceled out, making brand A the better choice. This is a good illustration of how other data should play a role in decision-making — a designed experiment doesn't exist in a vacuum.

This was a basic analysis to help you understand how interactions work. Minitab and other statistical analysis software run all of this analysis automatically, reducing the Six Sigma practitioner's workload. Most of that software also considers every possible interaction and presents the factors with the biggest impact in the analysis. If you have a 2^k factorial experiment with three factors, each with two settings, and those factors are A, B, and C, you could have the following possible effects on the outcome:

- A (the impact of changing only A)
- B (the impact of changing only B)
- C (the impact of changing only C)
- AB (the interaction of A and B)
- AC (the interaction of A and C)
- BC (the interaction of B and C)
- ABC (the interaction of all three factors)

Adding more factors makes this analysis increasingly complicated; adding more levels to each factor does too.

### 2^k Factorials versus Multi-Level Factorials

So far in this unit, every DOE scenario used has been a two-level (or 2^k) factorial experiment. In each experiment, Six Sigma teams chose to set each factor's levels at a maximum of two — typically a high and a low.

Why would a Six Sigma team choose to do this? Wouldn't an experiment with multiple factor levels provide the team more information? In the popcorn example, why would the team choose the high and low temperature settings? What happens when temperature is set at 500 degrees F? Or 425, 450, 475, etc.? How does the team know that 400 and 600 are the two most optimal settings?

The truth is the team doesn't know those are the most optimal settings, but adding multiple levels for one or more factors increases the number of runs that need to be completed. One replication of the popcorn experiment described earlier required eight runs. Just adding one more temperature factor — 500 degrees F — adds four runs to the experiment.

*(Table: 12 runs combining Brand (A, B), Temperature (400°F, 500°F, 600°F), and Kernels (1 scoop, 2 scoops) — a three-level factorial for temperature.)*

Now, instead of 32 runs for a designed experiment that includes four replications, the team would have 48 runs. That's 16 additional runs where the team's and the company's time and resources are being used. If the team also wanted to test the temperature settings of 425, 450, 475, 525, 550, and 575, that would mean 24 additional runs per replication, or 96 additional runs for four replications. If the team also decided to add more levels to other factors, like a third brand or trying 1.5 scoops of kernels, the team could be looking at an experiment with hundreds of runs needed to reach the appropriate sample size.

For these reasons, 2^k factorial experiments are typically the most commonly used among Six Sigma practitioners. Minitab lets you run these experiments with up to 15 different factors, providing a powerful ability to analyze processes. Minitab also lets you run experiments with more than two factors.

Experiments with multiple factors are handled much the same way as 2^k factorial experiments. Obviously, if you're handling the analysis manually, you'll want to limit the levels and factors as much as possible. Minitab removes the need to limit data because of analysis requirements — as long as the team can define a need to include factors and levels in an experiment and has gotten permission and access to use the resources needed to run an appropriate number of replications for accurate statistical conclusions, then Six Sigma teams can certainly run experiments with multi-level factors.

### Tips for Building Successful Designed Experiments

As with almost any other tool in the Six Sigma space, ANOVA and design of experiments are only as strong as the foundation you build each time you run an experiment and the associated analysis. Beyond the instructions and information in this unit, this section provides some tips for successful experiments and analysis.

**Take Time to Think About Your Experiment's Y, or Response**

In Chapter 73, defining the experiment's Y, or response, is one of the first steps in the procedure for running a DOE. Remember, a good response ties to the overall DMAIC process or the overall need associated with the experiment. The team should know what it wants to address and whether the response it's considering is a good measurement.

Often, Six Sigma training materials or DOE tips provide two common pieces of advice:

- Make sure the Y is continuous for later analysis purposes
- Pull the Y from brainstorming or other work done in earlier phases — specifically from Define or Analyze tools, like fishbone diagrams

While both are good advice, Six Sigma teams shouldn't be afraid to think outside the box when it comes to an experiment's response. At the end of the day, the response needs to be something that'll help you actually understand what you set out to understand at the start of the experiment.

In the popcorn experiment used as an example in this chapter, the team could have chosen any number of responses. Possible responses for the popcorn-popping process could include how long the overall process took, how many kernels popped, how many orders each process generated, or customer satisfaction with the popped popcorn's flavor. But the team wasn't seeking answers to questions related to production efficiency or product performance with this particular experiment. The team was asking questions about raw-material waste, and the amount of unpopped kernels told the team exactly how much waste was created in the process.

When considering an appropriate Y for your experiment, don't get too attached to the current metrics a process or department uses to measure success. The concession stand probably never considered unpopped popcorn before this experiment — it probably used sales figures or sales value as its success metric. If you're having trouble identifying a Y you think will help answer the questions the team is asking, consider running a fresh brainstorming exercise focused solely on arriving at an appropriate outcome type.

**Plan Ahead, and Keep Excellent Documentation**

You've seen throughout this unit that experiments and ANOVA analysis can get complex quickly. First, you have to validate every assumption, select the right method, and choose an appropriate sample size. Then, you have to run the experiments and log all the data. Finally, you have to run the analysis. At any point in the process, you can introduce an error or create confusion. Planning and documentation are essential to prevent that from happening, and they can be just as important when you present your experiment's conclusions to others. Some specific areas where documentation matters especially are highlighted below.

- Take notes while working through the ANOVA steps from Chapter 50 or the DOE steps from Chapter 73. At some point, you'll forget or mix up some number or element of the analysis, and you'll need to check your notes. Consider logging:
- Your reasons for choosing a specific method or test.
- Lists of responses, inputs, factors, and levels, with a reason for choosing each one. You might need that information to justify the number of runs in your experiment.
- The process for choosing sample size and any data or assumptions used in that process.
- Log any external assumptions made regarding the experiment, the experiment's components, or the outcome. You might need to revisit those assumptions or the data tied to them to rule out outliers or understand what might otherwise look like unexplainable experiment behavior.
- Document any instructions or information given to any operator within the experiment. Your sponsor or other decision-makers will likely want to understand exactly how the experiment was carried out before making decisions based on the results.
- The outcome of any measurement system analysis, particularly regarding confidence in the experiment's results.

**Account for Confidence Levels**

In any kind of statistical analysis, test, or DOE, the Six Sigma practitioner is always mindful of confidence levels. There's always some chance of a wrong conclusion — the alpha and beta errors covered in the hypothesis-testing chapters tell us that. More precise data, larger sample sizes, and choosing the right test or experiment help reduce the chance of these errors, but decision-makers need to know how large that possibility of error might be.

When reporting a designed experiment's outcome, make sure to account for every confidence level. The confidence interval for the actual experiment isn't always the only relevant consideration. Did you make assumptions based on earlier analysis to set up the experiment? What were the confidence intervals associated with that analysis? Consider the popcorn example again: how certain is the team that each scoop contains, on average, 2,300 kernels? What's the variation in that measurement? The answers to those two questions feed into the precision of the experiment's analysis.

If company leadership or a Six Sigma team is going to base resource-heavy decisions, or resource-dependent decisions, on a DOE analysis, then those decision-makers need to know how confident the Six Sigma practitioner is in what they're presenting. You should always do everything statistically possible to increase confidence — like validating data and assumptions and choosing adequate sample sizes — but you should never artificially inflate confidence in a conclusion to encourage leadership to support a given decision.

**Use Multiple Analyses and Experiments Together**

You shouldn't — and often can't — do everything you want in a single experiment. If there are 25 possible factors, do you really want all of them in a single, unwieldy experiment that could become expensive to run and impossible to control? Often, when you're considering running an experiment with that many factors, you're actually trying to fold multiple experiments into one. Stop and consider the possibility that you're comparing apples to oranges in one experiment, when you should actually be running separate experiments for various product types or processes.

If you're genuinely working on a single product type or process, consider that you might need to run experiments in a series. You might need to find out a given piece of information, or narrow down interactions and factors, to better set up other experiments with new factors and level settings. For example, the Six Sigma team in the popcorn example didn't finish their project just because they figured out how to best pop popcorn to reduce waste. There are other ways to increase profits. Since brand wasn't a major factor in the waste-related experiment, the team might run a second experiment to find out which brand customers prefer and whether increased customer satisfaction drives increased sales.

Designed experiments are one of the most challenging aspects of Six Sigma to learn, because exact rules don't always exist. Six Sigma teams can set up experiments in a variety of ways, which increases the tool's flexibility but can also make it hard to know exactly how to proceed. This is an area where experience pays off, so the more experiments and analyses you run, the better you get at setting up DOE. That's also a reason it's a good idea to work with a more experienced Six Sigma practitioner or a Master Black Belt, who can act as a sounding board for your ideas and guide you in building the best possible experiment.

### Excel and Power BI

This chapter already mentions that the main-effects charts in the text above were originally generated in Excel — and not by accident: calculating main effects and interactions in a $2^k$ factorial is, historically, one of the most natural spreadsheet-calculation examples, because it reduces to averages and differences of averages over coded $(-1/+1)$ columns.

```py-r
--- excel
' Efeito principal do fator A num 2^2 (coluna A codificada como -1/+1):
=SOMARPRODUTO((ColunaA=1)*ColunaY)/CONT.SE(ColunaA;1) - SOMARPRODUTO((ColunaA=-1)*ColunaY)/CONT.SE(ColunaA;-1)
' Efeito de interacao AB: cria-se uma coluna auxiliar ColunaAB = ColunaA*ColunaB
' e aplica-se a mesma formula do efeito principal sobre ColunaAB.
' O grafico de interacao (2 linhas, uma por nivel de B, com A no eixo X) e
' o proprio grafico de linhas nativo do Excel sobre as medias de celula.
```

For small, complete $2^k$ factorials, this manual Excel approach is sufficient and is exactly how DOE was taught and practiced before dedicated statistical software became widespread. As the number of factors grows (see the following chapters on fractional factorials and RSM), manually building the interaction columns becomes impractical, and the Python/R from the worked example becomes necessary.
